title: NASA Artemis II Fault-Tolerant Computer
source: How NASA Built Artemis Fault-Tolerant Computer.pdf

questions.prompt: What does a 'fail-silent' computer do when it detects an erroneous calculation?

options.text: It stays silent rather than transmitting the wrong answer
It transmits the wrong answer with a warning flag
It averages its result with the others

questions.explanation: A faulty computer fails silent rather than transmitting the wrong answer; self-checking pairs detect errors immediately.

questions.prompt: How many CPUs effectively run the Orion flight software in parallel?
questions.explanation: Two Vehicle Management Computers each contain two Flight Control Modules (four FCMs), and each FCM is a self-checking pair of processors — eight CPUs total.

questions.prompt: Instead of a triplex majority 'voting' mechanism, how does Orion select an output among healthy channels?

options.text: A priority-ordered source selection algorithm picking the first available FCM
A random choice among the FCMs

questions.explanation: Orion uses a priority-ordered source selection algorithm among healthy (non-silenced) channels, picking the first available FCM in the priority list.

questions.prompt: Orion uses a time-triggered Ethernet network with an ARINC653-compliant scheduler, dividing flight software execution into major and minor frames.
questions.explanation: A strictly deterministic, time-triggered Ethernet architecture with major/minor frames and an ARINC653 scheduler ensures each FCM sees the same inputs and produces the same outputs.

questions.prompt: Which hardware-level fault tolerance measures does Orion employ?

options.text: Triple-modular-redundant memory that self-corrects single-bit errors on every read
Network interface cards with two lanes constantly compared
A triple-redundant network with three separate planes
A single shared clock with no recalibration

questions.explanation: Orion uses TMR self-correcting memory, dual-lane compared NICs, and a triple-redundant network with three planes; clocks are recalibrated every second to network 'true' time.

questions.prompt: The Backup Flight Software (BFS) is an example of which principle?
questions.explanation: The BFS is a prime example of dissimilar redundancy: different hardware, different OS, and independently developed simplified software to avoid common-mode failures.

questions.prompt: According to the article, Orion can lose three FCMs in 22 seconds and still ride through safely on the last FCM.
questions.explanation: Uitenbroek states they can lose three FCMs in 22 seconds and still ride through safely on the last FCM; silenced FCMs can reset, re-synchronize, and rejoin.

questions.prompt: Which modern verification technique does NASA use to emulate flight timelines with injected hardware failures?

options.text: Large-scale fault injection on high-performance supercomputers

questions.explanation: NASA uses full-environment simulations, Monte Carlo stress testing, and large-scale fault injection on supercomputers to verify the software can fail silent and recover.

questions.prompt: How did the Apollo Guidance Computer compare to Orion's architecture?

options.text: Apollo used a ~1-MHz processor with about 4 KB of erasable memory and relied on mechanical fallbacks
Apollo managed every safety-critical function in software, like Orion

questions.explanation: The Apollo Guidance Computer had a ~1-MHz processor and roughly 4 KB of erasable memory, with critical controls handled by manual/electromechanical means; Orion instead manages nearly all safety-critical functions in software.

questions.prompt: In a total power loss ('dead bus') scenario, what does Orion do once power is restored?

options.text: Enters safe mode, stabilizes, points solar arrays at the Sun, then orients its tail to the Sun for thermal stability before re-establishing communication
Immediately fires all thrusters at full power

questions.explanation: After a dead bus, Orion enters safe mode: it stabilizes, points solar arrays at the Sun to recover power, then orients its tail to the Sun for thermal stability before attempting to re-establish communication.

questions.prompt: Orion measures each FCM's drift every second and recalibrates its local clock to the network's 'true' time.
questions.explanation: Every second, the drift of each FCM is measured and its local clock recalibrated to the network's true time; a module missing its deadline is silenced, reset, and re-synchronized.

questions.prompt: Where does NASA specifically anticipate transient failures during the Artemis II mission?

options.text: During transit through the high-radiation Van Allen Belts

questions.explanation: NASA anticipates transient failures during the mission's transit through the high-radiation Van Allen Belts, which is why the redundancy is scaled for deep space.

questions.prompt: According to Riley, what must fail-silent logic be paired with to avoid catastrophic gaps?

options.text: Active monitoring such as another component or a watchdog timer

questions.explanation: Riley emphasizes that a silently failing component may go undetected unless monitored by another component or watchdog timer; error detection/recovery must be explicitly designed across layers.

questions.prompt: What did Riley say about modern Agile/DevOps approaches in relation to architectural discipline?

options.text: They prioritize iteration, which can challenge architectural discipline and let technical debt accumulate
They are required for deterministic lockstep execution
They were used to build the Apollo AGC

questions.explanation: Riley notes modern Agile and DevOps prioritize iteration, which can challenge architectural discipline so technical debt accumulates and resiliency suffers.
